notes: \cpara{The anecdote is from Diogenes Laertius (\textsc{Lives} VI.40), and the post's ``is said to have'' suits it: ``Plato had defined Man as an animal, biped and featherless, and was applauded. Diogenes plucked a fowl and brought it into the lecture-room with the words, `Here is Plato's man.' In consequence of which there was added to the definition, `having broad nails.'\,'' The division itself is in Plato's \textsc{Statesman}, where bipeds are divided ``into those which have feathers and those which have not.''}
\cpara{Argues that no list of shared traits fits all humans and only humans and also captures what they have in common: some traits are shared with other species, others belong to only some humans.}
\cpara{Credits the rough definition with a use: it picks out real examples.}
\cpara{The mechanism: from the examples, learn the other traits they share.}
\cpara{The result: the enriched category rejects the plucked chicken, whatever the definition says.}

\cpara{The foil describes Aristotle's logic of definition narrowly. Aristotle's rules reject a definition that fits something other than the thing defined: a definition ``ought to be peculiar'' to its object (\textsc{Topics} VI.1). By those rules the plucked chicken refutes ``featherless biped,'' as the Platonists in the story concluded. The rule also presupposes that one already knows the chicken is not a man, which is the post's point about recognition.}
\cpara{Adds pointing to the verbal clue, as in ``Extensions and Intensions.''}

\cpara{The thesis, and the post's term for it: a ``similarity cluster'' is ``the group of things that have many characteristics in common.'' The idea has a well-known predecessor that the post does not mention: Wittgenstein's ``family resemblances,'' ``a complicated network of similarities overlapping and criss-crossing'' (\textsc{Philosophical Investigations} \S\S 66--67). The next post cites the psychological research on ``prototype effects'' (Rosch and Lloyd, 1978).}
